paras: The lynching of Joseph Snyder took place on December 27, 1880, at Santee's Mills near Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, when a crowd took Snyder, accused of murdering Jacob and Anna Gogel, from a detective and hanged him from a chestnut tree. Newspapers called it the first lynching ever to occur in Pennsylvania, and it drew editorial condemnation in New York and across the state. Warrants were reported, but a grand jury later declined to take up the case.

Snyder, an ore miner aged 24 or about 28 whom the Daily Gazette described as 'a German by birth', boarded with the Gogel family. According to the Bethlehem dispatch in The Sun, he had made advances toward the Gogels' daughter Alice, and her father had ordered him to stop or leave. Jacob and Anna Gogel were found killed with an axe in their bed early on December 27, and the papers reported that Snyder had raised the alarm with a story of burglars before slipping away.

Detective W. W. Yohe of the Lehigh and Susquehanna Railroad led a search by about two hundred men and boys, and found Snyder hidden in the straw of George B. Ritter's barn. Yohe handcuffed him and brought him back to the Gogel house, followed by a crowd that yelled 'Hang him!' Inside, Yohe guarded the prisoner with a revolver while, by the Philadelphia Times account, a man named Eshlman told the crowd that a trial would cost thousands in taxes and Snyder might still escape.

When the Rev. D. F. Brendle of Bethlehem asked Snyder whether he had done it, Snyder was reported to have answered yes. While Coroner Uhler and his jury were upstairs holding the inquest on the Gogels, the crowd pushed the detective aside, put a rope around Snyder's neck and dragged him out of the house and across the road to a chestnut tree. The Sun counted about 100 people on the rope, the Carbon Advocate put the crowd at 150 to 200, and the Philadelphia Times named John Mack, a Bethlehem shoemaker, as the man who climbed the tree.

The jury that had sat on the Gogels met that evening in Bethlehem and found that Snyder died by hanging 'at the hands of persons unknown to the jury', and his body was taken to the county poorhouse. District Attorney Anstett was reported to have issued warrants for twelve participants but to fear that no jury would convict, and farmers were said to have threatened to resist any arrests. By January 6 an Easton dispatch reported that his term had ended with nothing done, that he had said his own father took part, and that public opinion opposed prosecution.
In February Judge Myers told the grand jury that 'Snyder's death was murder', but the Northampton County grand jury did not take up the case.

The first Allentown wire, printed the same day in Lancaster and Washington and the next day in Richmond and Sacramento, said only that Snyder had been 'caught by an infuriated mob' and that the motive was unknown. Fuller accounts followed in The Sun, whose reporter reached the scene that morning, and in the Philadelphia Times, reprinted by the Juniata Sentinel. The Wilmington Daily Gazette headlined its Easton account 'The First Lynching Ever Known in Pennsylvania'.

Editorials framed the case as Eastern lawlessness. The New-York Tribune wrote that 'Judge Lynch' had set up court in Pennsylvania and that the participants were guilty of murder. The Lancaster Intelligencer called the crowd's offense 'the most heinous one that the law can know', questioned parts of the story told against Snyder, and replied to papers near the scene that resented outside criticism. The Lancaster Express answered that the lynchers had acted from 'a natural impulse of horror', the Clearfield Republican said the act could 'find no justification', and the Juniata Sentinel blamed lenient courts.

Accounts differ over how long Snyder hung, from twenty minutes in the second Allentown wire to three-quarters of an hour in the Philadelphia Times, and over who cut him down. Reports also differ on who did the hanging, naming miners, Bethlehem people or the leading men of the neighborhood.

bases: A crowd took Joseph Snyder, accused of killing Jacob and Anna Gogel, from Detective Yohe's custody and hanged him from a chestnut tree near Bethlehem, Pennsylvania (A13, A19, A47).

A crowd of about 100 (The Sun) to 150-200 (Carbon Advocate) seized Snyder from an officer and hanged him without legal process as punishment for the alleged double murder; a coroner's jury found he died by hanging at the hands of persons unknown, and Judge Myers called his death murder (A19, A42, A13, A58).
The Sun, the Philadelphia Times, the Easton account in the Wilmington Daily Gazette and the Carbon Advocate independently describe the seizure from custody and hanging (A19, A47, A13, A42).

accounts.label: First Allentown wire
accounts.gist: Snyder, the Gogels' boarder, 'believed to be the murderer', was caught by an infuriated mob and hanged to the nearest tree; motive unknown.

accounts.label: Second Allentown wire
accounts.gist: Found in a barn at 9 a.m., Snyder confessed to Brendle that he killed the parents to remove opposition to his suit, was hanged from a chestnut tree for twenty minutes; the detective fired at a ringleader.

accounts.label: Bethlehem dispatch (The Sun, Lancaster Intelligencer)
accounts.gist: A Sun reporter at the scene describes Yohe's arrest, the crowd entering while the coroner's jury was upstairs, two hoistings and about 100 hauling the rope.

accounts.label: Philadelphia Times dispatch
accounts.gist: A detailed version naming 'Edward Snyder' describes a crowd of several hundred, Eshlman's harangue, a club blow, the murdered man's brother, John Mack climbing the tree and three-quarters of an hour of hanging.

accounts.label: Easton account (Daily Gazette)
accounts.gist: Places the hamlet east of Easton, calls Snyder German-born, reports the 'persons unknown' verdict and that Easton citizens were divided.

accounts.label: Carbon Advocate
accounts.gist: Women did most of the shouting; the leading men of the neighborhood took a hand; officers knew the participants but sympathy was with the lynchers.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune said 'Judge Lynch' had set up court in the East and called the act murder without extenuating circumstances.
The Lancaster Intelligencer called the lynchers' offense 'the most heinous one that the law can know' and questioned parts of the story against Snyder.
The Lancaster Intelligencer's paragraph of Dec. 28 called Snyder a 'monster' and said Judge Lynch held court above the Mason and Dixon line.
The Lancaster Express called the lynchers men moved by 'a natural impulse of horror' and mocked calls to punish them.
The Clearfield Republican said the act 'can find no justification' and someone should be held responsible.
The Juniata Sentinel blamed lenient courts for 'the uprising and lynching of Snyder'.
Distant papers ran the Allentown wires under headlines such as 'Murder and Lynching' and 'Double Murder and Lynch-Law'.
